# DAG Scheduling in Waves

Given a plan whose subtasks declare `depends_on`, release **every** subtask whose dependencies are
already finished, all at once, as one parallel wave. When they rejoin, do it again. Repeat until
nothing is left. It is a topological sort executed in batches rather than one node at a time, and the
batch is the point: the width of each wave is the parallelism available for free.

## Why batches rather than a queue

A worker pool with a ready-queue gets the same throughput, but the *wave* is a unit the user can be
shown. In [[agent-orchestrator]] each release emits one event —

```
{"event":"wave", "data":{"ids":[…], "index":0, "size":3}}
```

— so the panel can say "three agents started together" instead of three unrelated starts a
half-second apart. Scheduling that is legible costs nothing here and buys the whole progress display.

## The two bugs this shape invites

**Counting the wave by its subtasks.** `schedule()` runs once per rejoining worker, not once per
wave, so numbering waves by how many ids had been dispatched labelled a two-wave plan `0` then `2`.
The fix is a counter incremented on release, not derived from the work.

**Running out of supersteps.** `schedule → worker → schedule` is a loop, so each wave costs two
[[langgraph]] supersteps. The library's default `recursion_limit` of 25 aborts a deep plan partway
through — which looks like a model failure and is not. The project sets 150.

## What makes a wave safe

Two subtasks in the same wave are independent *by construction* — that is exactly the property that
makes running them together correct. It is also what makes context sharing decidable: a subtask may
see its transitive ancestors and nothing else, because nothing else is guaranteed to exist yet
([[transitive-context-with-budgets]]).

The scheduler must therefore be defensive about the plan it is given, since the plan comes from a
model: dependency ids that name nothing are dropped rather than deadlocking the run, and a cycle is
broken rather than looped on. A DAG asserted by an LLM is a DAG only until it isn't.
